sources: Li et al. 2005, PLoS Genetics 1(1): e3, "Pseudogenization of a Sweet-Receptor Gene Accounts for Cats' Indifference toward Sugar": the cat Tas1r2 gene has a 247-base pair microdeletion and stop codons and no detectable expression, so cats most likely cannot detect sweet-tasting compounds; the same defect was found in tiger and cheetah; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1183522

Humphrey, Proops, Forman, Spooner & McComb 2020, Scientific Reports 10:16503, "The role of cat eye narrowing movements in cat-human communication": cats were more likely to approach an unfamiliar experimenter after a slow blink than after a neutral expression; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7536207/
title: Your Cat Most Likely Can't Taste Sugar 🐱 (Things Living In Your House #64)
description:
Why doesn't your cat care about sweets? In cats, one gene of the sweet taste receptor (Tas1r2) is broken, so cats most likely can't taste sugar, and tigers and cheetahs carry the same broken gene. In a 2020 study, cats were more likely to approach a person who slow blinked at them.

#shorts #cats #catfacts #thingslivinginyourhouse #meatballmyths

Sources: Li et al. 2005, PLoS Genetics; Humphrey et al. 2020, Scientific Reports.
